paragraphs: What our sages of blessed memory instituted, the Kaddishes of Shacharit, their purpose is as follows: prayer serves to rectify and elevate the worlds of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah. From the beginning of the prayer until 'Baruch She'amar' one is in the world of Asiyah; from there until 'Yotzer Or' in the world of Yetzirah; from there until the Amidah in the world of Beriah; and the Amidah itself is in Atzilut. Afterward one descends from above to below, since on weekdays we lack the strength to sustain the worlds in the elevation performed for them except momentarily, and immediately they return to their place. Thus from 'Ashrei' until 'Tefillah LeDavid' (Psalm 86) one is in Beriah, from there until 'Ein Kadosh KaHashem' in Yetzirah, and from there until 'Aleinu LeShabeach' in Asiyah. Therefore they instituted a Kaddish between each world and the next, for through the Kaddish - constructed according to the secret meaning in the number of its words and letters - the ascent of the worlds above their own level is completed; and for this reason all its words came to be as they are, as well as the five initial craftsmen/artisans [phrases] within it, corresponding to a known and precise number needed for the ascent of the worlds. And the Kaddish was instituted in the Aramaic translation-language so that the klipot (husks) too should not ascend together with the worlds' ascent, to attach themselves to them and draw sustenance from them for the time being - for they recognize and understand the Aramaic language, and when they hear this great, awesome, and holy praise of the Kaddish, they become subdued and do not ascend. Moreover, through our intention in the Kaddish, the spark of holiness - the vitality within the klipot - departs, ascends above, and joins with holiness, and through this there is a very great subduing of the klipot, and 'all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.' Therefore it is said in the holy Zohar concerning the Kaddish that it 'breaks iron chains,' as is mentioned in the Sefer HaKavanot of our teacher the Arizal, and blessed memory, and in the book Pardes of Rashi, of blessed memory. In siman 6 he gave another reason for why it was instituted in Aramaic, but the primary reason is that of the Arizal. And why Kaddish is not said before the Amidah we shall explain further on, with God's help.

clarification.explanation:
What our sages instituted as the Kaddishes of Shacharit - their meaning, according to the secret: prayer rectifies and elevates the worlds of Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah. From the start of the prayer until 'Baruch She'amar' - in the world of Asiyah; from there until 'Yotzer Or' - in Yetzirah; from there until the Amidah - in Beriah; and the Amidah - in Atzilut; and afterward one descends from above to below, since on weekdays we lack the strength to sustain the worlds in elevation except momentarily, and they immediately return to their place (from 'Ashrei' until 'Tefillah LeDavid' [Psalm 86] in Beriah, until 'Ein Kadosh KaHashem' in Yetzirah, until 'Aleinu LeShabeach' in Asiyah). Therefore they instituted a Kaddish between one world and the next, so that through the Kaddish - constructed according to the secret in the number of its words and letters (and likewise the first five 'craftsmen' phrases within it) - the ascent of the worlds above their level is completed.
And they instituted the Kaddish in the language of Targum (Aramaic), so that the klipot too should not ascend in the worlds' ascent to attach themselves and draw from them - for they understand the Aramaic language, and when they hear this great and awesome praise they become subdued and do not ascend; furthermore, through our intention in the Kaddish, the spark of holiness (the vitality) within the klipot departs and ascends to join with holiness, and this is a great subduing of the klipot. Therefore it is said in the Zohar concerning the Kaddish that it 'breaks iron chains.' All this is from the Sefer HaKavanot of the Arizal, of blessed memory; and the reason Kaddish is not said before the Amidah will be explained elsewhere.
takeaways: Prayer elevates the four worlds (Asiyah, Yetzirah, Beriah, Atzilut), and the Kaddish between one world and the next - constructed according to the number of its words - completes their ascent.

The Kaddish is in Aramaic so that the klipot (which understand Targum) become subdued and do not ascend with the worlds; and through the intention of the Kaddish the spark of holiness within the klipot ascends - hence it 'breaks iron chains.'

paragraphs: From 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' until 'Be'alma' there must be, according to the secret, twenty-eight words; and if one says only 'Mikol Birchata' there are here only twenty-seven words. Therefore our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, wrote that one must say 'Min Kol' to complete the twenty-eight. And as for what our teacher and master Rabbi Shmuel Vital, of blessed memory, questioned in his gloss on Sha'ar HaKavanot regarding the recitation of 'Min Kol' - in my holy books Rav Pe'alim I raised great objections to his words, and there I brought the verse 'and let them bless Your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise' (Nehemiah 9:5); and according to the words of our teacher and master Rabbi Shmuel Vital, of blessed memory, one would have had to say here 'Mikol.' There too I brought a parallel to the recitation of 'Min Kol' in Scripture, in Daniel 1: 'and fatter in flesh than all the youths' (verse 15), and likewise in the Aramaic language it is found there in chapter 2: 'in the wisdom that is in me more than all the living' (verse 30), and likewise in chapter 7: 'which shall be different from all the kingdoms' (verse 23).

clarification.explanation: From 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' until 'Be'alma' there must be, according to the secret, twenty-eight words; and if one says only 'Mikol Birchata' there are only twenty-seven. Therefore one must say 'Min Kol Birchata' to complete the twenty-eight, as the Rashash wrote (and this is also proven from the wording of verses and from the Aramaic of the Book of Daniel).
takeaways: In the Kaddish one says 'Min Kol Birchata' (not 'Mikol') in order to complete the count of twenty-eight words, which carries a secret meaning.

paragraphs: The mitzvah of answering the Kaddish response 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' is that the one answering must hear the beginning of the Kaddish, namely the two words 'Yitgadal VeYitkadash,' since 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' is the response to 'Yitgadal.' Therefore, ideally, the whole congregation should pay attention to hear the entire Kaddish from the word 'Yitgadal,' in order to have proper intention for what they are answering. However, an individual who entered the synagogue [late], or who finished the Amidah and found the congregation answering Kaddish, may answer with them. And only regarding the recitation of the 'Amen' that precedes 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' is there a dispute: some say one should begin answering from 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' and not say that 'Amen,' since it would be considered an 'orphaned Amen'; and some say one may also answer that 'Amen,' and it is not considered an orphaned Amen. And in my holy book Makbetziel I concluded that whoever acts either way has grounds to rely upon - for those who answer 'Amen' have support to rely on - and so it is fitting to instruct.

clarification.explanation: The mitzvah of answering the Kaddish ('Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach') requires that the one answering hear the beginning of the Kaddish, the two words 'Yitgadal VeYitkadash,' since 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' is the response to 'Yitgadal'; therefore, ideally, the whole congregation should pay attention to hear the Kaddish from 'Yitgadal,' in order to have intention for what they are answering. Nevertheless, an individual who enters the synagogue [late], or who finished the Amidah and found the congregation answering Kaddish, may answer with them. And only regarding the 'Amen' that precedes 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' is there a dispute: some say one should begin answering from 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' and not say that 'Amen' (which is considered an 'orphaned Amen'), and some say one may also answer 'Amen,' and it is not an orphaned Amen. The Ben Ish Chai (in Makbetziel) concluded that whoever acts either way has grounds to rely upon, and those who answer 'Amen' have support, and so it is fitting to instruct.
takeaways: The mitzvah of answering Kaddish is to hear from 'Yitgadal VeYitkadash' and have intention; 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' is the response to 'Yitgadal.'

One who enters in the middle and finds the congregation answering may answer with them; regarding the 'Amen' preceding 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' there is a dispute, but in practice one who answers 'Amen' has grounds to rely upon.

paragraphs: If they began saying Kaddish with ten present and some of them left, they finish that Kaddish, provided that a majority remains; but if a majority does not remain, they do not [finish]. Either way, of those who left it is said, 'and they that forsake the Lord shall be consumed' (Isaiah 1:28). And if ten remain there is no problem. And if there were ten present during the recitation of the passage of the daily offering and the sacrifices and the Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael, and some of them left, one may not say Kaddish unless ten remain. The same law applies if there were ten present during the Zemirot and the Song of the Sea and some left before the Kaddish began - one may not say Kaddish with fewer than ten. Likewise, if there were ten present during the recitation of Ashrei before Minchah and some of them left before the Kaddish began, one may not say it with fewer than ten, even though these Kaddishes are obligatory, as the reason is mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch of our teacher Rabbi Zalman [Baal HaTanya], of blessed memory, siman 58, se'if 4.

clarification.explanation: If they began saying Kaddish with a quorum of ten and part of them left - they finish the Kaddish if a majority remains (though those who left deserve reproach, 'and they that forsake the Lord shall be consumed'); if the majority does not remain, they do not finish it. Likewise, if there was a quorum during the recitation of the sacrifices/the passage of the daily offering/Zemirot/Ashrei before Minchah, and they left before the Kaddish itself began - one may not say Kaddish with fewer than ten, even though these Kaddishes are obligatory.
takeaways: A Kaddish that began with ten and the quorum diminished - they continue if a majority remains.
If the quorum broke before the Kaddish itself began - it is not said with fewer than ten.

paragraphs: If there are exactly ten present and one of them is praying the Amidah and cannot answer Kaddish with them, he nevertheless counts toward the quorum. The same law applies even if two, three, or four are praying [the Amidah], so long as a majority remains who answer Kaddish and Amens, it is permitted to say Kaddish - for wherever there are ten, the Divine Presence rests upon them and they may say a matter of holiness, which is not so regarding the chazan's repetition, which differs, as will be explained further on, with God's help. However, if one of the ten is asleep, some say that with one asleep alone they may say Kaddish, but not with two, since it is not respectful of Heaven to count two sleeping men; and some say that one should not compare a sleeping person to one who is praying, since a sleeping person has a partial withdrawal of the soul and holiness does not rest upon him, but rather, on the contrary, a degree of impurity rests upon him, even if he is sleeping during the day - therefore he may not be counted even alone. And so it is fitting to instruct: even with one person asleep, they should not say Kaddish until they wake him; and if it is not possible to wake him, they should not say it.

clarification.explanation: If there were exactly ten and one of them is praying the Amidah and cannot answer Kaddish - he nevertheless counts toward the quorum; the same applies even if two, three, or four are praying, so long as a majority who answer Kaddish and Amens remains, it is permitted to say Kaddish, since wherever there are ten the Divine Presence rests and they may say a matter of holiness (unlike the chazan's repetition, as will be explained). But if one of the ten is asleep - some say a single sleeping person may be counted, but not two (since it is not respectful of Heaven to count two sleeping men); and some say one should not compare a sleeping person to one who is praying, since a sleeper has a certain withdrawal of the soul and holiness does not rest upon him, but rather a degree of impurity (even sleeping by day), and therefore not even one may be counted. And so it is fitting to instruct: even with one asleep, they should not say Kaddish until they wake him, and if it is impossible to wake him, they should not say it.
takeaways: Ten present in exact number, with one (or several) praying the Amidah - they count toward Kaddish, so long as a majority who can answer remains.
A person asleep in the quorum - in practice is not counted (since there is a withdrawal of the soul); wake him, and if that is not possible, do not say Kaddish.

paragraphs: A deaf-mute who can speak but not hear, or who can hear but not speak, is regarded like one of sound senses and counts toward any matter of holiness, even though he does not answer with them; and even if there are three or four such persons, so long as a majority of those present answer, they count toward the quorum - except for the chazan's repetition of the Amidah, for which nine who hear the repetition and answer Amen are required, as will be explained further on. But one who neither hears nor speaks is regarded like a deaf-mute of the kind the Sages everywhere spoke of, comparable to an imbecile or a minor, and does not count. Likewise, one under a ban of excommunication (menudeh) and a mourner before burial (onen) do not count toward any matter of holiness. But a transgressor who violated a communal decree under a ban - since he was not explicitly excommunicated - does count. And a drunkard, if he is unable to speak coherently in the presence of a king, does not count.

clarification.explanation: A deaf-mute who speaks but does not hear, or hears but does not speak, counts toward the quorum for a matter of holiness (even though he does not actually answer), so long as a majority of those present answer; but for the chazan's repetition, nine who hear and answer Amen are required. One who neither hears nor speaks is like an imbecile or a minor and does not count. One under a ban and a mourner before burial do not count; a transgressor who was not explicitly excommunicated does count; a drunkard who cannot speak coherently before a king does not count.
takeaways: A deaf-mute (who hears or speaks, not both) counts toward an ordinary quorum, but not toward the chazan's repetition.
One under a ban, a mourner before burial, and a severely intoxicated person do not count toward the quorum.

paragraphs: All ten must be in one place, with the chazan, who is counted among them, also present with them; but if some are in one room and some in another, they do not combine even if there is an open doorway between them. As for the platform (teivah or bimah) in the synagogue on which the chazan stands - even though it is ten handbreadths high, quite wide, and has partitions ten handbreadths high - the chazan still counts together with them and fulfills their obligation on their behalf, because this platform is nullified in relation to the synagogue, being made for the synagogue's purpose. Now this requirement, that all ten be in one place, applies specifically to the matter of forming the quorum; but if there are ten in one place saying Kaddish or Kedushah, anyone who hears their voice - even one standing in another house, even if there are several houses between him and them - may answer Kaddish with them, provided nothing separates between him and them such as filth or a gentile [standing in between]. And this ruling, that filth or a gentile constitutes a separation preventing one from answering, applies when one is standing in another house, whose law is that he does not combine with them [for the quorum, but may still answer if he hears]; but if he is standing in the same place [as the congregation], even if there is a gentile standing in that very place, he still answers with the congregation Kaddish and Kedushah and every matter of holiness. And the people must be warned about this matter, for gentiles are often found standing at the entrance of the synagogue selling some item, and people walking in the alley outside the entrance, behind the gentile, who hear Kaddish and the like, should not answer. But if the gentile has entered into the synagogue itself, it makes no difference, and the whole congregation within the synagogue answers every matter of holiness, even those standing behind the gentile.

clarification.explanation: All ten (including the chazan) must be in the very same place; if some are in a different room, they do not combine even if there is an open door between them. The platform in the synagogue is considered nullified in relation to the synagogue and does not constitute a separation. One who hears the sound of Kaddish/Kedushah from another house may answer along with them (provided there is no interruption of filth or a gentile standing in between - but if he is in the same place as the congregation, even if a gentile is present there, he does answer). And the people must be warned about this: sometimes gentiles stand at the entrance of the synagogue to sell something, and one who stands in the alley outside the entrance - behind the gentile - and hears Kaddish, does not answer. But if the gentile enters into the synagogue itself, the entire congregation inside answers, even those standing behind him.
takeaways: The quorum must be in the very same place; but one who hears from another house may answer (provided there is no interruption of filth/a gentile in between).
A gentile standing at the entrance of the synagogue interrupts for one standing outside; once the gentile enters inside, everyone answers.

paragraphs: A Kaddish that one was already standing for, such as the Kaddish after the Amidah, and after Hallel, where one was standing at its start, should remain standing until after the full response of 'Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabba.' Likewise, one must be careful with any Kaddish where it happens that one was sitting when the Kaddish began, and an elder or Torah scholar passed by and one rose out of respect for him - he should remain standing until after the response of 'Amen, Yehei Shmei Rabba,' since once he has already stood, it is considered as though the Kaddish caught him standing.

clarification.explanation: A Kaddish in which one was standing from the outset (such as after the Amidah or after Hallel) - one remains standing until the end of the response 'Amen Yehei Shmei Rabba.' Likewise, one who was sitting and rose out of respect for an elder or Torah scholar in the middle of the Kaddish is considered as one whom the Kaddish 'caught standing,' and remains standing until the end.
takeaways: A Kaddish that began while standing (or during which one rose) - one remains standing until the end of 'Amen Yehei Shmei Rabba.'

paragraphs: Just as one must be careful about an unnecessary blessing, so one must be careful not to multiply Kaddishes unnecessarily. However, if one studied the Written Torah and wishes to say the Kaddish 'Yehei Shlama,' and afterward studied the Oral Torah and says the Kaddish 'Al Yisrael,' or vice versa, there is no problem, since this is not considered multiplying Kaddishes. Therefore the custom here in our towns is to say every day, after the fixed study of the Oral Torah, the Kaddish 'Al Yisrael,' and afterward to study Tehillim (Psalms) and say the Kaddish 'Yehei Shlama.' And the same is done on the night of the festival of Shavuot and on Hoshana Rabbah. And I have heard that in the Holy City as well, their custom on these two nights is to say a Kaddish after the Written Torah, and a Kaddish after the Oral Torah.

clarification.explanation: Just as one is careful about an unnecessary blessing, so one is careful about multiplying Kaddishes; but a Kaddish after studying the Written Torah and then after studying the Oral Torah (or vice versa) is not considered multiplication, and so the custom developed of saying the Kaddish 'Al Yisrael' after Oral Torah study, and afterward studying Tehillim and saying 'Yehei Shlama' (and likewise on the night of Shavuot and Hoshana Rabbah).
takeaways: A separate Kaddish after Written Torah study and after Oral Torah study is not considered an unnecessary multiplication of Kaddishes.

paragraphs: Just as it is forbidden to pass in front of one who is praying, so it is forbidden to pass in front of one who is saying Kaddish, as is written in Birkei Yosef; see also Minchat Aharon, page 61, column 3. However, it appears that if the one saying Kaddish has reached 'Al Yisrael' and there is a need to pass in front of him, it is permitted; and so we are accustomed to practice.

clarification.explanation: Just as it is forbidden to pass in front of one who is praying, it is forbidden to pass in front of one saying Kaddish; but if the one saying Kaddish has reached 'Al Yisrael' and there is a need to pass, it is permitted.
takeaways: One should not pass in front of the one saying Kaddish, unless he has already reached 'Al Yisrael' and there is a need.

paragraphs: 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' is the Aramaic translation of 'May His great Name be blessed.' Therefore one should connect the word 'Mevarach' with the word 'Rabba,' pronouncing 'Mevarach' with a kamatz under the bet and a patach under the reish, so that its meaning is as though it read 'Mevorach' [passive, 'is blessed'], as is mentioned by the later authorities. And one should pronounce the first tav of 'Tushbechata' [further in the Kaddish] with a chirik. Also, when one says 'Le'alam Ul'almei Almaya,' one should connect the word 'Yitbarach' with the word 'Almaya,' so as not to pause between 'Almaya' and the word 'Yitbarach.' See Magen Avraham siman 66, se'if katan 6, and Ma'amar Mordechai siman 56, se'if katan 6, and Shalmei Tzibbur, page 84, column 4. Also, the one answering Kaddish must be careful to pause slightly between 'Amen' and 'Yehei Shmei Rabba,' since that 'Amen' refers to what precedes it, and the praise begins from 'Yehei Shmei.' And the one answering Kaddish must be careful to answer with all his strength - meaning, with all his intention - and also to raise his voice somewhat, but not louder than the voice of the one saying the Kaddish, just as the law for one answering Amen is that he may not raise his voice louder than the one reciting the blessing, as mentioned in Chesed LeAlafim. And the response of Kaddish takes precedence over the response of Kedushah if both arrive for the listener simultaneously; but if one has already begun answering Kedushah, one should not stop in order to answer Kaddish. Likewise, if one has already heard and answered one Kaddish, but has not yet heard Kedushah that day, then in that case the response of Kedushah takes precedence, so that one fulfills the obligation of both Kaddish and Kedushah, as mentioned in Chesed LeAlafim. And if two people are saying Kaddish, one ahead and one behind, one should answer after the one who is ahead.

clarification.explanation: 'Yehei Shmei Rabba Mevarach' is the Aramaic translation of 'May His great Name be blessed' - one should connect 'Mevarach' with 'Rabba' (bet with kamatz, reish with patach), and likewise pronounce the first tav of 'Tushbechata' (later in the Kaddish) with a chirik; and when saying 'Le'alam Ul'almei Almaya,' one should connect the word 'Yitbarach' with 'Almaya' without pausing between them. The one answering Kaddish should pause slightly between 'Amen' and 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' (since that Amen belongs to what precedes it, and the praise begins from 'Yehei Shmei'), and should answer with all his strength (his intention), raising his voice slightly but not more than the one reciting. The response of Kaddish takes precedence over Kedushah if both come together; but if one has already begun answering Kedushah, one should not stop to answer Kaddish. And if one has already heard and answered one Kaddish that day and has not yet heard Kedushah, the response of Kedushah takes precedence, so as to fulfill the obligation of both Kaddish and Kedushah.
takeaways: Precise points of pronunciation in 'Yehei Shmei Rabba' and further in the Kaddish.
Kaddish takes precedence over Kedushah if they arrive together; but if one has already begun Kedushah, one does not stop.

paragraphs: According to the words of our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory: the Kaddish before 'Hodu' and before 'Yotzer,' and the one after the Amidah before 'Ashrei,' and the one before 'Tefillah LeDavid,' and the one before 'Pittum HaKetoret' - all five of these are obligatory, and a minor may not say them alone on behalf of the congregation; rather, an adult is required to fulfill the congregation's obligation with them. And the Kaddish that precedes 'Aleinu LeShabeach,' said after 'Tana DeVei Eliyahu,' is called the 'Orphan's Kaddish' (Kaddish Yatom), which our Sages instituted for orphans to say; it is not included among the five aforementioned Kaddishes instituted for the sake of the worlds, but rather this Kaddish belongs to the world of Asiyah, and is of benefit to the deceased if his son says it within twelve months, and also on every anniversary of the death (yahrzeit). It has two benefits: one, to save him from the judgment of Gehinnom; and the other, to bring him into Gan Eden and raise him from level to level. Therefore the orphans say it within the twelve months, and also on the day of the yahrzeit each and every year. And so it was the practice of our teacher the Arizal, may the memory of the righteous be a blessing, to say this final Kaddish every year on the anniversary of his father's passing, both in Shacharit and in Arvit, as is mentioned in Sefer HaKavanot, see there. And I found written in the handwritten book Keter Malchut that the orphan should say quietly, whether within the twelve months or on the day of the yahrzeit each year, before this Kaddish, verses from the alphabet beginning with the letters of the name of his father or mother for whom he is saying this Kaddish - for each letter of their names he should say one verse specifically, quietly - and its reasoning is pleasing to me, and so it is fitting to do, for the matter is reasonable and there is no loss in it.

clarification.explanation: According to the Arizal, five Kaddishes in the Shacharit prayer are obligatory (before 'Hodu,' before 'Yotzer,' after the Amidah before 'Ashrei,' before 'Tefillah LeDavid' [Psalm 86], before 'Pittum HaKetoret'), and only an adult (not a minor) may say them on behalf of the congregation, for the sake of rectifying the worlds. But the Kaddish before 'Aleinu LeShabeach' (after 'Tana DeVei Eliyahu') is called the 'Orphan's Kaddish' - instituted specifically for orphans, and is not among the five main Kaddishes; it has two benefits for the deceased: rescue from the judgment of Gehinnom, and elevation through the levels of Gan Eden. Therefore the orphan says it during the first twelve months and on every anniversary (yahrzeit).
takeaways: The five main Kaddishes of Shacharit - for the rectification of the worlds - are said specifically by an adult.
The Orphan's Kaddish (before Aleinu LeShabeach) is specifically for orphans, helping the deceased escape Gehinnom and ascend in Gan Eden.

paragraphs: Here in our city, may it be built and established, the custom is to say in this final Kaddish, both in Shacharit and in Arvit, 'Rabbanan, bless the Lord who is blessed.' But in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and established speedily in our days, the custom is not to say 'Rabbanan,' and each community should follow its own custom in this matter. And in my holy book Rav Pe'alim I gave, with Heaven's help, a reason for the recitation of 'Rabbanan,' both here and before the blessing over the Torah at the Torah reading.

clarification.explanation: In Baghdad the custom is to say in the Orphan's Kaddish (in Shacharit and Arvit) 'Rabbanan, bless the Lord who is blessed,' but in Jerusalem the custom is not to say 'Rabbanan'; each community follows its own custom.
takeaways: Saying 'Rabbanan Barchu' in the Orphan's Kaddish is the custom of Baghdad; Jerusalem does not follow this custom.

paragraphs: The Gaon Chida wrote in Shiyurei Berachah, siman 376, se'if katan 8, that according to what our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory, wrote - that the Kaddish also serves to elevate his soul - it would seem that one should say Kaddish for the full twelve months. However, on account of the common people, one reduces the final week, as the Rav Kenesset HaGedolah wrote, siman 403, that since they were concerned lest it appear as though they were saying that the wicked are judged in Gehinnom for twelve full months, whatever one reduces from the twelve months is sufficient - so far his words. And here in our city of Baghdad the custom follows this: at the completion of the eleventh month they hold an additional study session and go to the grave, calling that day 'the incomplete year,' and after that they stop for one week at the beginning of the twelfth month. And although the Rav wrote that one stops in the last week of the eleventh month, it makes no difference, for it amounts to the same thing. And all this concerns stopping the Kaddishes that the orphans say; but the Kaddish said after study, which every person says, they too continue to say. There is also a custom here among us that if the day of the yahrzeit falls in the middle of the week, the orphans begin saying the Kaddishes from the Shabbat night before - that is, from the Arvit prayer of Shabbat - until the end of Minchah of the yahrzeit day; and if the yahrzeit falls on Shabbat itself, they begin from the Arvit of the preceding Shabbat and say it throughout the week until the end of the second Shabbat, which is the yahrzeit day. This custom is cited in Shalmei Tzibbur, page 190, column 2. But from the Sefer HaKavanot it appears clearly that our teacher the Arizal, of blessed memory, would say Kaddish for his father only on the single day of the yahrzeit itself, at night and during the day. And know that the meaning of 'yahrzeit' is 'day of passing' in the Ashkenazic language, and the Sephardim too have become accustomed to calling it by this name in their books, and it is not an acronym or any other hint as some people think.

clarification.explanation: According to the Arizal, the Kaddish also helps elevate the soul of the deceased, and so it would be proper to say it for the full twelve months; but for the sake of the common people (so that it should not appear as though the deceased is judged as wicked in Gehinnom for a full year) they stop one week before the year's end. In Baghdad: they stop at the beginning of the twelfth month (a day called 'the incomplete year,' with additional study and a visit to the grave). Regarding a yahrzeit Kaddish that falls in the middle of the week, they begin saying it already from the Shabbat before. And this stopping applies only to the Kaddishes said by the orphans, but the Kaddish said after study - which every person says - continues to be said by them as well. And from Sefer HaKavanot it appears that the Arizal himself said Kaddish for his father only on the day of the yahrzeit itself, night and day. And 'yahrzeit' means 'day of passing' in the Ashkenazic language, and it is not an acronym or hint, as many people suppose.
takeaways: Orphan's Kaddishes for the deceased are said throughout the year minus one week (to avoid giving a negative impression).
Baghdad custom: begin saying the yahrzeit Kaddishes from the preceding Shabbat if the yahrzeit falls in the middle of the week.
The stopping applies only to the orphans' Kaddishes; the Kaddish said after study continues to be said.

paragraphs: Regarding a deceased person who has no offspring, or whose son is a minor, and they hire someone to say Kaddish on his behalf, I was asked in my holy book Rav Pe'alim whether this is of avail in such a case, and I wrote, with Heaven's help, there, that I found it written - as cited in Beit Yosef at the end of the section Yoreh De'ah - implying that they had an ancient custom of hiring a person to say Kaddish for the soul of the deceased. This is also proven from the responsum of Maharik, of blessed memory, root 44, see there. And see the book Chayim BeYad, siman 114, what he wrote as the reason for the custom of the mother-city in Israel, Izmir, may it be built and established, of giving the final Kaddish said before 'Aleinu LeShabeach' to the rabbi and teacher of the city, see there. And in the book Kisei Eliyahu, printed in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be built and established, he wrote regarding the rectification of a fast day, that one should bring others to fast along with him, see there. And I wrote that in any case, one who says Kaddish for the dead who are strangers to him should say each day, at the end of the day, this request: 'May it be Your will... that You have pity, compassion, and mercy, in the abundance of Your mercies and kindnesses, upon the nefesh, ruach, and neshamah of So-and-so son of So-and-so, and for the sake of the Kaddishes that I, Your servant, have said this day, may You nullify all accusers and prosecutors, and may righteous advocates arise to speak well on behalf of his nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, and may peace accompany them, and may they dwell in the tranquility of peace, quiet, and security, and may You increase Your kindnesses over the attribute of judgment, and may the harsh judgments be sweetened through the supreme wonder, which is great kindnesses and complete mercies, may they be favorable, etc.'

clarification.explanation: A deceased person without offspring, or whose son is a minor, for whom one hires a person to say Kaddish on his behalf - this is of avail, as is proven from ancient sources. One who says Kaddish for a deceased person who is a stranger to him should say, at the end of each day, a special request asking for mercy upon the soul of the deceased, that by virtue of the Kaddishes he said the accusers be nullified and there be peace and rest for his soul.
takeaways: Hiring a person to say Kaddish for a deceased person without a son is an ancient and effective custom.
One who says Kaddish for a stranger's deceased adds a personal request at day's end on behalf of his soul.

paragraphs: In my holy book Rav Pe'alim I was asked about four or five people saying Kaddish together, one of whom has such a low voice that no one in the congregation hears his voice, whether it is necessary for him to say Kaddish along with those saying it whose voice the congregation does hear alone. There I brought the words of the Rav Emet LeYaakov, in the laws of the blessings for those called up to the Torah, page 24, letter samech. I also brought the words of the Rav Binyan Tziyon, siman 122, who cast doubt on this. I further brought the testimony of the Rav, the eminent and pious Gaon, Mahara Mani, may his light shine, regarding the custom of the pious in Beit El, may it be established and firm, that the chazan alone says the Kaddish with proper intentions (kavanot), and if there is someone in the congregation who has a yahrzeit and wishes to say Kaddish, he says it quietly, so as not to disturb the chazan's intention. He also testified that in the book Petach HaDevir, siman 125 [not available to us], it is likewise written that this makes no difference. Nevertheless, I concluded that ideally one should not act this way, and that the aforementioned custom of the pious ones is different, because it is not otherwise possible there. I was further asked there about ten people who studied Tehillim and all wish to say Kaddish, such that not a single one answers - and I brought the words of the Rav Benei Yehudah Ayash, of blessed memory, siman 3, and elaborated somewhat on this, and concluded that ideally they should be careful that one person answer the Kaddish for them.

clarification.explanation: Several people saying Kaddish together, one of whom has such a low voice that no one in the congregation hears him - the Ben Ish Chai concluded that ideally one should not act this way; and the custom of Beit El (that the chazan alone says it aloud with intention, and one with a yahrzeit says it quietly) is exceptional, since it is not otherwise possible there. Likewise, ten who studied Tehillim and all wish to say Kaddish without anyone answering - ideally, they should be careful that one person answers the Kaddish for them.
takeaways: Ideally, several people should not say Kaddish together when one's voice is inaudible to the congregation; the custom of Beit El (the chazan alone aloud, and the one with a yahrzeit quietly) is exceptional because there is no other way there. And with ten who studied Tehillim - they should be careful that one person answers for them.
